sections.heading: C — Conveyance, Signals, Railroad, Work Zones
sections.markdown:
## C — Conveyance, Signals, Railroad, Work Zones

FACT_ID: sec04-F01 | anchor: A01
A twenty twenty-four Iowa law orders drivers to yield crosswalk right-of-way to people on foot and to riders of any human-powered device, called a pedestrian conveyance [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0010]

FACT_ID: sec04-F02 | anchor: A01
A conveyance is any human-powered device used to get around without walking or to move another person, including wheelchairs, strollers, skateboards, scooters, and electric personal assistive mobility devices [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0010]

FACT_ID: sec04-F03 | anchor: A01
Every use of the word pedestrian in the manual covers both walkers and conveyance riders [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0010]

FACT_ID: sec04-F04 | anchor: A02
A reflective orange triangle on a vehicle's rear means it travels at thirty-five miles per hour or less, as seen on maintenance rigs, farm vehicles, and horse-drawn wagons [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F05 | anchor: A02
Guide signs give directions and distances to cities, airports, borders, parks, and museums, while mile markers count miles from the state line for exit math and emergency location [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F06 | anchor: A02
Service signs point to rest areas, fuel, campgrounds, and hospitals [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F07 | anchor: A02
A route sign's shape reveals its road type, interstate, federal, state, or county, so follow those signs to hold your route [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F08 | anchor: A02
Officers, highway workers, and school crossing guards may direct traffic, and you must follow their directions [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F09 | anchor: A02
Solid red orders a complete stop, while flashing red is handled exactly like a stop sign [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F10 | anchor: A02
On solid yellow, hold back when you can stop safely and otherwise clear the intersection with care [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F11 | anchor: A02
Flashing yellow means advance with caution, yielding to vehicles and pedestrians until the way is safe [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F12 | anchor: A02
Solid green means go only when the way is clear, yielding to anyone still inside and letting trapped traffic clear after the change [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F13 | anchor: A02
A steady red arrow forces turning drivers to stop [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F14 | anchor: A02
A steady yellow arrow warns the turn signal is going red, so hold back when stoppable and finish the turn only from inside the intersection [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F15 | anchor: A02
A flashing yellow arrow lets you turn left after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, since the opposing lanes hold green [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F16 | anchor: A02
A steady green arrow permits the indicated turn while oncoming traffic waits, yet forbids going straight and still requires giving way to anyone already inside [A02].
Why it matters: the green arrow protects the turn but never the straight path.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0011]

FACT_ID: sec04-F17 | anchor: A03
Treat every rail crossing with extra care and never halt on the tracks, since trains cannot brake fast and advance signs plus pavement markings announce the rails ahead [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F18 | anchor: A03
Near the tracks, drop distractions, roll the windows down, and silence the music so you can sense a train [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F19 | anchor: A03
Each crossing posts its railroad name with an emergency number to call for signal faults, stalls, obstructions, or track damage [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F20 | anchor: A03
At gated or lighted crossings, flashing lights or lowered gates mean a train is coming, so obey them and never cross or weave around a gate [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F21 | anchor: A03
Passive crossings show only a crossbuck with a stop or yield sign, so slow down, look for the train, and always expect one [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F22 | anchor: A03
School and charter buses, hired-ride drivers, and placarded hazmat haulers must halt fifteen to fifty feet before the rails, then cross; an officer's or signal's order to proceed and a posted EXEMPT sign both excuse the stop [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F23 | anchor: A03
Stalled on the tracks with a train near, keep cranking the starter until the train shows, stand clear waving at the engineer, then get everyone out at once and walk clear of the rails at a forty-five-degree angle toward the oncoming train [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F24 | anchor: A03
Cross tracks only at marked crossings, heed every sign and signal, and remember that ungated tracks still carry trains announced by advance signs and markings [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F25 | anchor: A03
Rail cars wear reflective stripes for night and murky weather, so scan for the train itself before rolling across [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F26 | anchor: A03
Always expect a train, which may run closer and faster than it looks on any track at any time, with extra tracks meaning extra trains, so confirm a clear view both ways first and never try to beat one [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F27 | anchor: A03
Cross only when sure of clearing fully, since trains overhang the rails; when waiting, keep fifteen feet between your vehicle and the closest rail, and never shift gears mid-crossing [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F28 | anchor: A03
Stuck or stalled at a crossing, empty the vehicle and run far even with no train in sight, then phone the blue-and-white ENS sign's number with its crossing ID, or call emergency services at nine-one-one when no sign stands [A03].
Why it matters: the ENS call and the nine-one-one fallback are the only sanctioned summons.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0012]

FACT_ID: sec04-F29 | anchor: A04
The page after the rail-crossing rules holds an illustrated guide to rail signs and signals credited to Operation Lifesaver [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec04-F30 | anchor: A05
Work zones add arrow boards, temporary signals, flaggers, and channelizing hardware, with mostly diamond-shaped orange signs and only a few rectangles [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec04-F31 | anchor: A05
Those devices mark construction, maintenance, survey, and utility work, steering drivers and walkers past the crew; stay sharp because fines may double there [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec04-F32 | anchor: A05
In work zones, match speed to conditions, obey every sign, signal, and flagger, stretch your following gap, and lock your full attention on driving [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec04-F33 | anchor: A05
Big flashing arrow panels usually signal a closed lane or shoulder [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec04-F34 | anchor: A05
Flaggers with stop-or-slow paddles direct work traffic and must be obeyed; they wear fluorescent yellow-green or orange and mostly use paddle signs, with red flags only at times [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec04-F35 | anchor: A05
Barricades, upright panels, drums, cones, and tube markers warn of odd or risky layouts and funnel drivers safely through [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-ia-c:iowa-department-of-transportation-iowa-d:handbook:pdf-0014]

Misconceptions: flashing red is a stop sign while flashing yellow only asks caution; a steady green arrow still requires giving way to traffic already inside; passive crossings carry no lights or gates at all, so looking is the only protection.

Mnemonic: solid red stops, flashing red stops too; yellow means decide, green means go when clear; arrows add turning rules to the same colors.

Glossary: conveyance (a human-powered device counting as a pedestrian, from wheelchairs to scooters); active crossing (rails guarded by lights or gates); passive crossing (rails marked only by a crossbuck with a stop or yield sign); channelizing device (a cone, drum, or barrier steering traffic through work); flagger (a vest-wearing worker directing traffic with paddles).

Dynamic facts: none in these pages; every rule above is stable handbook knowledge with no date-variable or place-variable values.
